titulo: Introductions, countries, numbers 0 to 20 and age: Countries and nationalities

aula.titulo: Introductions, countries, numbers 0 to 20 and age
aula.objetivo: Introduce yourself and others, name countries and nationalities, count from 0 to 20 and say your age with «avere». Choose between «tu» and «Lei», and avoid the three classic English-speaker traps: «sono bene», «sono venti anni» and a capital letter on nationalities.

blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: most countries take a definite article in Italian: «il Brasile», «la Francia», «la Spagna», «gli Stati Uniti». English leaves it out («Brazil», «France»), except in a few cases like «the United States». STEP 2: the article changes with the gender and first sound of the country. After a vowel, it shrinks to «l'»: «l'Italia», «l'Inghilterra», «l'Argentina». STEP 3: nationalities are adjectives, and they are not written with a capital letter: «italiano», «francese». English capitalizes them («Italian», «French»); Italian does not. STEP 4: the adjective changes with the gender of the person: «italiano» (man), «italiana» (woman); «americano», «americana». STEP 5: adjectives ending in «-e» are the same for both: «francese», «inglese», «portoghese». STEP 6: to say where you are from, use «Sono» and the nationality: «Sono brasiliano» (a man), «Sono brasiliana» (a woman). STEP 7: pronunciation: «gn» in «Spagna» and «spagnolo» is like «ny» in «canyon». «Gli» in «gli Stati Uniti» is like «lli» in «million». In «Germania» and «Inghilterra», «g» before «e» and «i» sounds like «j»; «gh» in «Inghilterra» is a hard «g».
blocos.comparacao: English has no grammatical gender, so «American» is the same for a man and a woman. Italian marks the difference in the ending: «americano» and «americana». Capital letters work the other way round: English capitalizes nationalities and Italian does not. And the article before a country name is the third change: English says «I live in Italy», Italian often keeps the article in other sentences («l'Italia è bella»).

erros.motivo: Nationalities are written in lowercase in Italian.
The adjective agrees with a woman: «americana».

itens.explicacao: Listen to the start: «Fran-» is France; the ending «-ese» is the nationality.
In «Inghilterra», «gh» is a hard «g», as in «get».

itens.explicacao: Nationalities are lowercase in Italian, even though English capitalizes them.
The ending «-a» marks a woman; «argentino» is for a man.
Adjectives in «-e» do not change between man and woman.
Italian «gn» is one soft nasal sound: «SPAH-nyah».

blocos.enunciado: Say where you are from, in Italian, using «Sono» and your nationality. If you are a woman, check the ending. Then say where a friend of yours is from.
Say the ten countries and their adjectives aloud. Which of them end in «-e»? Which change between «-o» and «-a»?
